fields.h1: Build a Credit Card Authorization Form Customers Sign Online
fields.hero_description: Create a credit card authorization form that sends card numbers to Stripe and saves each signature to a database you own.
fields.features_heading: What a Credit Card Authorization Form Must Say
fields.features_subheading: Every authorization ties one card to a charge the cardholder agreed to. These six features build that record.
fields.feature_1:
The fields every authorization carries

Emergent asks for the cardholder's name and billing address, the card brand and expiration date, what the charge covers and the amount, then a signature, and the signing date.
fields.feature_2:
Card numbers go to Stripe, not your inbox

Customers type the card number into Stripe's payment fields. Your table keeps the card brand, the last four digits and a Stripe customer ID, enough to bill the card again.
fields.feature_3:
One-time, recurring, or card on file

Pick the kind of authorization and the form adapts. A single charge asks for an amount. A recurring one adds a billing day and an end date. A card on file lists its fees.
fields.feature_4:
A signature tied to the exact wording

Customers sign on screen with a finger or a mouse. The record keeps the signature next to the terms exactly as they read then. Editing the terms later leaves old records alone.
fields.feature_5:
Each charge points to its authorization

Every charge made against a saved card is logged under the signed form that allowed it. When a customer disputes one, the signed form and the charge history sit on one record.
fields.feature_6:
Source code you can hand to a developer

On paid plans, export the full codebase to GitHub when someone wants invoicing or a client portal. The form and its Stripe connection go with it, plus every stored authorization.

fields.tab_content_1:
Room and tax only, up to $640

Booking a room for someone else at the Harbor Inn starts with one link. The cardholder names the guest and chooses what the card covers: room and tax for two nights, capped at $640. Incidentals stay with the guest. The front desk sees the signed authorization on the reservation before check-in.
fields.tab_content_2:
Retainers go through on the 1st without a phone call

Clients of Ledgerline Bookkeeping sign once for a $1,500 monthly retainer and save a card in Stripe. Each card is charged on the 1st, and the charge is logged under that client's authorization. When a card declines, the account manager gets a Slack message with the client's name and the amount due.
fields.tab_content_3:
A missed visit triggers the fee they signed for

Patients who book online at Northside Physical Therapy save a card and accept one rule: missing a visit without 24 hours' notice costs $50. When the front desk marks a no-show, one click charges the fee to the saved card. The patient gets an emailed receipt quoting the policy they signed.
fields.tab_content_4:
The rep never hears the card number

Phone orders at Copper Kettle Roasters end with an email instead of digits read aloud. The rep enters the order, and the buyer authorizes a one-time charge of $2,340 from a link on their phone. The rep sees only the card brand and last four digits. Once it is signed, the order goes to the warehouse.

fields.howto_title: How to Build a Credit Card Authorization Form
fields.howto_description: Seven steps to a credit card authorization form that states the exact charge and never asks for the security code.
fields.howto_step_2_title: 02 Write the terms the cardholder signs
fields.howto_step_3_title: 03 Keep the security code off the form
fields.howto_step_1_des: Decide whether the card pays once, on a schedule or only after something happens, like a missed appointment. That choice sets what the cardholder signs for. Keep one type per form so the customer knows exactly what they agreed to.
fields.howto_step_2_des: Put the amount, how often it is charged and how to cancel in plain sentences above the signature line. Use your business name as it appears on card statements. The cardholder can then match each charge to the form they signed.
fields.howto_step_3_des: Card rules bar a business from keeping the CVV once a charge is authorized. Leave that box off entirely and let Stripe collect the card. The full number then never sits in an inbox or a filing cabinet.
fields.howto_step_4_des: Tell Emergent who signs, what the card covers and which details you need from the customer. Include your authorization wording exactly as your terms state it. Emergent builds the form and the table that stores each signed record.
fields.howto_step_5_des: Connect Stripe so a card can be saved at signing without charging it. Recurring and on-file charges then run against the saved card. Each one is recorded next to the signed terms, which is where you look first when a customer questions a charge.
fields.howto_step_6_des: Decide who acts when a charge fails. Send that person a Slack message or an email with the customer's name, the amount, and a link to the record. The customer can receive a link to update the card at the same moment.
fields.howto_step_7_des: Put Stripe in test mode and sign the form as a made-up customer using one of Stripe's test card numbers. Confirm the record holds the signature and only the last four digits. Then have someone outside the team read the terms before a real customer signs.
